ap_chemistry-f01.title: Permanganate titration of iron in an ore

stimulus.description: A student dissolves a $1.000\text{ g}$ sample of iron ore in acid so that all of the iron is present as Fe²⁺ and dilutes the solution to $100.00\text{ mL}$. A $25.00\text{ mL}$ portion is titrated with $0.0300\text{ M}$ KMnO₄. The balanced equation is MnO₄⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H₂O. The endpoint is reached after $21.60\text{ mL}$ of KMnO₄ has been added.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of MnO₄⁻ added at the endpoint and the number of moles of Fe²⁺ in the $25.00\text{ mL}$ portion.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the moles of MnO₄⁻ (about 6.480e-04 mol)
common_errors: uses the volume in mL without converting to liters

rubric_rows.criterion: Multiplies by 5 for the moles of Fe²⁺ (about 3.240e-03 mol)
common_errors: uses a 1:1 mole ratio

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percent of iron in the ore sample.
parts.model_answer: The 100.00 mL solution holds 4 × 3.240e-03 = 1.296e-02 mol Fe, which is 0.7238 g; mass percent = 0.7238/1.000 × 100 = 72.4%.

rubric_rows.criterion: Scales the moles of Fe²⁺ from the 25.00 mL portion to the 100.00 mL solution (about 1.296e-02 mol)
common_errors: uses only the moles in the 25.00 mL portion

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the mass percent of iron by converting to the mass of iron and dividing by the ore mass (about 72.4%)
common_errors: divides by the mass of the portion instead of the whole sample

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: No indicator was added to the flask. Explain how the student can still identify the endpoint.
parts.model_answer: MnO₄⁻ is purple and is reduced to nearly colorless Mn²⁺ while Fe²⁺ remains; once all of the Fe²⁺ has reacted, the first excess drop of MnO₄⁻ leaves a faint persistent pink color.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the endpoint is the first persistent pink or purple color
common_errors: says the solution becomes colorless at the endpoint

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that MnO₄⁻ is consumed (reduced to colorless Mn²⁺) until the Fe²⁺ is gone, so the excess MnO₄⁻ colors the solution
common_errors: says Fe²⁺ itself produces the pink color

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A bubble was trapped in the tip of the buret before the titration and left the tip during the titration. Will the calculated mass percent of iron be too high, too low, or unaffected? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Too high: the bubble volume is counted as titrant delivered, so the recorded volume is larger than the volume that reacted.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the mass percent of iron will be too high
common_errors: says it will be too low

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the buret reading overstates the volume of KMnO₄ that reacted, which overstates the moles of Fe²⁺
common_errors: says the concentration of KMnO₄ changes

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Identify the oxidizing agent in the reaction and justify your answer using oxidation numbers.
parts.model_answer: MnO₄⁻ is the oxidizing agent: the oxidation number of Mn decreases from +7 to +2, so MnO₄⁻ is reduced and oxidizes Fe²⁺.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies MnO₄⁻ as the oxidizing agent
common_errors: identifies Fe²⁺ as the oxidizing agent

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites the change in the oxidation number of Mn from +7 to +2, showing that it is reduced
common_errors: uses the oxidation number of iron without noting that it increases

ap_chemistry-f02.title: Electrolysis of copper sulfate solution

stimulus.description: A student electrolyzes $1.0\text{ M}$ CuSO₄(aq) between two inert electrodes, using a constant current of $2.00\text{ A}$ for $60\text{ minutes}$. Copper metal forms on one electrode, and a gas forms on the other. Use F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate the total charge, in coulombs, and the number of moles of electrons that flow.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the charge (7200 C) using the time in seconds
common_errors: uses the time in minutes

rubric_rows.criterion: Divides by the Faraday constant (about 0.0746 mol e⁻)
common_errors: multiplies by the Faraday constant

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of copper that forms.
parts.model_answer: Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu, so n(Cu) = 0.0746/2 = 0.0373 mol and the mass is 2.37 g.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses two moles of electrons per mole of Cu (about 0.0373 mol Cu)
common_errors: assumes one mole of electrons per mole of Cu

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the mass of copper (about 2.37 g)
common_errors: omits the molar mass

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The gas formed at the other electrode is O₂, from 2 H₂O → O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻. Calculate the volume of O₂ at 298 K and 1.00 atm.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses four moles of electrons per mole of O₂ (about 0.01866 mol)
common_errors: uses two moles of electrons per mole of O₂

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the volume of O₂ with PV = nRT (about 0.456 L)
common_errors: uses the temperature in °C

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Identify the electrode at which copper forms and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Copper forms at the cathode: Cu²⁺ gains electrons and is reduced, and reduction occurs at the cathode.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the electrode at which copper forms as the cathode
common_errors: identifies the anode

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with Cu²⁺ gaining electrons (reduction), which occurs at the cathode
common_errors: says oxidation occurs at the cathode

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The student repeats the electrolysis with the current doubled. Predict the time needed to deposit the same mass of copper and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Half as long: the same mass requires the same charge, q = It, so doubling the current halves the time.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the time needed is half as long
common_errors: says the time stays the same

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the same mass needs the same total charge and q = It
common_errors: says the mass depends only on the current

ap_chemistry-f03.title: Method of initial rates and the rate law

stimulus.description: Initial rates for A + B → products at one temperature

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to A and with respect to B. Justify each answer with the data.
parts.model_answer: Doubling [A] with [B] fixed multiplies the rate by 4, so the order in A is 2; doubling [B] with [A] fixed multiplies the rate by 2, so the order in B is 1.

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the order 2 in A by comparing experiments 1 and 2 (rate ratio 4)
common_errors: compares experiments in which both concentrations change

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the order 1 in B by comparing experiments 1 and 3 (rate ratio 2)
common_errors: uses the coefficient from the equation

rubric_rows.criterion: Relates each rate ratio to the factor by which the concentration changed
common_errors: gives the orders without using the data

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Write the rate law for the reaction and calculate the value of the rate constant, including units.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes rate = k[A]^2[B]^1
common_errors: includes a product or a concentration with the wrong exponent

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates k (about 0.04 M⁻² s⁻¹) with units
common_errors: omits the units of k

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial rate when [A]₀ = 0.3 M and [B]₀ = 0.15 M.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes the concentrations into the rate law
common_errors: uses the concentrations of experiment 1

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the rate (about 5.400e-04 M/s)
common_errors: adds the terms instead of multiplying

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The temperature is increased and the experiments are repeated. The rate constant increases. Explain this increase in terms of the molecules that react.
parts.model_answer: A larger fraction of collisions has energy at least equal to the activation energy at the higher temperature, so more collisions are effective and the rate constant is larger.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that a larger fraction of collisions has enough energy to react
common_errors: says the activation energy decreases

rubric_rows.criterion: Connects the energy to the activation energy at the higher temperature
common_errors: says the concentration of the reactants increases

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: A student proposes that the reaction occurs in a single elementary step A + B → products. Is the proposal consistent with the rate law? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Not consistent: for a single elementary step the rate law would be rate = k[A][B], which does not match the experimental orders 2 and 1.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the proposal is not consistent because an elementary step has orders equal to its coefficients, rate = k[A][B]
common_errors: decides from the coefficient of the overall equation without considering the experimental orders

ap_chemistry-f05.title: Gravimetric analysis of chloride

stimulus.description: A student dissolves a $0.600\text{ g}$ sample of an unknown chloride salt in water and adds excess AgNO₃(aq). The AgCl precipitate is filtered, washed, dried, and found to have a mass of $1.250\text{ g}$. The molar mass of AgCl is 143.32 g/mol, and the molar mass of Cl is 35.45 g/mol.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the precipitation reaction.
parts.model_answer: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) with phases
common_errors: includes spectator ions in the equation

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of AgCl formed and the mass of chloride in the sample.

rubric_rows.criterion: Divides the mass of AgCl by its molar mass (about 0.00872 mol)
common_errors: multiplies by the molar mass

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the moles of Cl⁻ equal the moles of AgCl (1:1)
required_elements: moles of Cl- equal moles of AgCl
common_errors: uses the mole ratio of the salt instead of the chloride

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the mass of chloride (about 0.3092 g)
common_errors: uses the molar mass of AgCl

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percent of chloride in the unknown salt.

rubric_rows.criterion: Divides the mass of chloride by the mass of the sample
common_errors: divides by the mass of the precipitate

rubric_rows.criterion: Expresses the result as about 51.5%
common_errors: leaves the result as a fraction

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A student forgets to dry the precipitate completely before finding its mass. Predict the effect on the calculated mass percent of chloride, and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Too high: wet precipitate has extra mass from water, so the mass of AgCl is too large and the moles of Cl⁻ are overestimated.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the mass percent will be too high
common_errors: says the result will be too low

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that the extra water adds mass to the precipitate, overstating the moles of AgCl and Cl⁻
common_errors: says the water reacts with the chloride

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The student repeats the experiment but uses too little AgNO₃(aq), so some chloride remains in solution. Explain why the calculated mass percent would be incorrect.
parts.model_answer: Too low: AgNO₃ would be the limiting reactant, so less AgCl forms than the chloride in the sample could produce.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the calculated mass percent would be too low
common_errors: says the result would be unaffected

rubric_rows.criterion: States that not all of the chloride precipitates, so the mass of AgCl underestimates the chloride in the sample
common_errors: says the excess AgNO₃ lowers the mass of AgCl

ap_chemistry-f06.title: Galvanic cell, free energy and the Nernst equation

stimulus.description: A galvanic cell is built from a Cu electrode in Cu²⁺(aq) and a Fe electrode in Fe²⁺(aq), connected by a salt bridge. The standard reduction potentials are Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu, E° = +0.34 V, and Fe²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Fe, E° = -0.44 V. Use F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻ and E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q at 25 °C.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate the standard cell potential, E°cell, and identify the anode.
parts.model_answer: E°cell = 0.34 − (-0.44) = 0.78 V; Fe is oxidized, so Fe is the anode.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates E°cell by subtracting the reduction potentials (about 0.78 V)
common_errors: adds the reduction potentials

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the Fe electrode as the anode
common_errors: identifies Cu as the anode

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the standard free energy change, ΔG°, in kJ per mole of reaction.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses n = 2 moles of electrons
common_errors: uses n = 1

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates ΔG° of about -151 kJ/mol with the correct sign
common_errors: omits the negative sign or leaves the units in J

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the cell potential when the reaction quotient is Q = 10.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes E° and Q into E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q
common_errors: uses the natural logarithm

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates E of about 0.750 V
common_errors: adds the correction term

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Describe the direction in which electrons and anions in the salt bridge move in this cell.
parts.model_answer: Electrons move through the wire from the Fe anode to the Cu cathode; anions move through the salt bridge toward the anode compartment to balance the charge as Fe²⁺ forms.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that electrons flow from the Fe electrode to the Cu electrode
common_errors: says electrons move through the salt bridge

rubric_rows.criterion: States that anions in the salt bridge move toward the anode to balance the positive charge
common_errors: says anions move toward the cathode

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The concentration of Cu²⁺ in the cathode compartment is decreased. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The cell potential decreases: a smaller [Cu²⁺] increases Q, and E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q becomes smaller.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the cell potential decreases
common_errors: says the cell potential increases

rubric_rows.criterion: Links the lower [Cu²⁺] to a larger Q and a smaller E in the Nernst equation
common_errors: says E° changes with concentration

ap_chemistry-f07.title: Two-step mechanism, half-life and a catalyst

stimulus.description: The decomposition of a reactant X(g) → products occurs in two steps. Step 1 (slow): X → Y + Z. Step 2 (fast): Y → W. The reaction is first order in X with a rate constant k = 0.0347 min⁻¹ at a fixed temperature. The initial concentration of X is $0.8\text{ M}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the rate law for the overall reaction and identify the rate-determining step.
parts.model_answer: rate = k[X]; the slow first step X → Y + Z is the rate-determining step, and its rate depends only on [X].

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes rate = k[X]
common_errors: includes [Y] in the rate law

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the slow step (step 1) as rate-determining
common_errors: says the fast step determines the rate

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Identify an intermediate in the mechanism and explain how you know.
parts.model_answer: Y is an intermediate: it is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2, so it does not appear in the overall reaction.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies Y as the intermediate because it is produced in one step and consumed in a later step
common_errors: identifies the final product W as the intermediate

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the half-life of X and the time needed for the concentration of X to fall to 0.0625 of its initial value.
parts.model_answer: t½ = ln 2 / k = 20.0 min; t = ln(16)/k = 79.9 min.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses t½ = ln 2/k for a first-order reaction
common_errors: uses t½ = 1/(k[X]₀)

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the half-life (about 20.0 min)
common_errors: omits the units or uses log10

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the time to reach 0.0625 of the initial concentration (about 79.9 min)
common_errors: assumes a constant amount of reactant is consumed per half-life

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Calculate the concentration of X after 60 minutes.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses ln[X] = ln[X]₀ − kt or [X] = [X]₀ e^(−kt)
common_errors: uses the zero-order equation [X] = [X]₀ − kt

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates [X] of about 0.100 M
common_errors: omits the exponent's negative sign

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: A catalyst is added that provides a new pathway for the slow step. Explain the effect of the catalyst on the activation energy, the enthalpy change of the reaction, and the rate constant.
parts.model_answer: The catalyst lowers the activation energy of the slow step, so k increases; the enthalpy change is unchanged because the reactants and products are the same.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the activation energy decreases, the rate constant increases, and ΔH does not change
common_errors: says the catalyst changes ΔH

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that a lower barrier lets a larger fraction of collisions react and that ΔH depends only on the reactants and products
common_errors: says the catalyst is consumed in the overall reaction
